title: A small share of time
hookLine: how small a share of endless time is given to each of us (Meditations 12.32)

lines: A WHOLE LIFE UNDER YOUR THUMB.
cards: Open the photos on your phone and scroll back. A year. Five.
The faces get younger, the haircuts get worse, and somewhere in there is a day that seemed like it would never end. A whole life under one thumb. Marcus had no camera roll.
But near the end of his notebook, an emperor stops and measures a life, his own included, against all of time.

teach.h: MEASURE YOUR LIFE AGAINST ALL TIME.
teach.b: Meditations 12.32, in George Long's translation: "How small a part of the boundless and unfathomable time is assigned to every man?" He goes on: it's swallowed up in the eternal almost at once.
Then he widens the lens: how small a part of all matter, of the soul of the whole, of the earth you creep on. First, the measuring.

Marcus has done this all through the book: Asia and Europe as corners of the universe, the present as a point. Here he aims it at himself. An emperor, measured against endless time, holds a tiny slice.
So does everybody else. Second, why this isn't gloom.
The point of 12.32 isn't that your life is worthless. It's that your share is given. Long's word is assigned: handed out, like a ration.
You didn't earn it and you can't extend it. Which makes the question not how much do I have, but what do I do with the share in my hand. Third, what he does with it.

Right after the measuring, the passage turns: he tells himself to think nothing great except to act as his own nature leads, and to bear what the common nature brings. Small share, plain job. Fourth, the Tuesday version.
A day is a small share of a small share.

teach.h: A DAY IS A SHARE OF A SHARE.
teach.b: You can't fill it with everything.
You can fill it with a few things done as yourself, well. That's not shrinking your life. It's fitting your hands to it.

how: Readers of Marcus often use the view of endless time as a way of sorting a day, setting the small things down and choosing a few to do well.

o: a Roman poet who wrote about the shortness of summer
the emperor who said a long life is earned by virtue
the emperor who measured a life as a small, assigned share

games.q: a small share of time. tap the pairs.
p: how small a part of time each is given
act as your own nature leads
a small share of a small share

s: in 12.32 Marcus concludes that a human life is worthless
he says the share is small and given, then turns to how to use it.
Marcus measures not only time but matter, soul and the earth
he widens the lens to all matter, the soul of the whole, and the clod of earth we live on.
the emperor exempts himself from the measuring
he aims it at himself; his share is as small as anyone's.

games.q: you've just pictured your life as a tiny slice of endless time. what does Marcus do next in 12.32?
o: decide nothing matters and stop trying.
tell himself to act as his nature leads and bear what comes.
plan a monument so he'll be remembered.
games.why: the passage turns from measuring to a plain job: think nothing great except acting by your nature and bearing what the whole brings.

practice: Picture today as one small square on a very long ribbon of squares, before you and after you, and look only at yours: work, a meal, a person, a chore.
Pick one thing in it that matters to you, and decide to do it as yourself, with care. Then rest on the breath, a very small share of time, and enough for now.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who measured each life as a small, assigned share of boundless time, given, not earned. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an age, eternity. The endless time Marcus measures each life against.

carryVoice: Your line: a small share. Small, and still yours to use well. Day six hundred thirty-five, done.
